title: Overfitting and Underfitting
learning_outcomes: Explain overfitting and underfitting and accurately refer to at least two syllabus subtopics.
Apply the main idea of overfitting and underfitting to a small example, trace, calculation, or scenario.
Identify one important assumption or failure mode and describe how to check it.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will study overfitting and underfitting in the context of machine learning fundamentals. You will connect the PDF subtopics to a small example and practice describing what the evidence does—and does not—support.
content.why_it_matters: Overfitting and Underfitting matters because it affects how data is collected, represented, analyzed, interpreted, or used in a decision. Check the task and assumptions before choosing a method.

content_blocks.title: The central idea
content_blocks.text: Machine learning estimates patterns from examples. Training is only one step: a robust workflow defines splits, baselines, metrics, assumptions, and monitoring.

items.title: Model complexity
items.text: Define model complexity in relation to overfitting and underfitting; identify the input, output, assumptions, and who uses the result.

items.title: Generalization
items.text: Work through generalization using a small, synthetic example before scaling up. State what the calculation or method returns and why that result is useful.

items.title: Bias–variance trade-off
items.text: Check the edge cases for bias–variance trade-off: missing values, unusual ranges, different groups, time boundaries, or a changed input can affect the conclusion.

items.title: Learning curves
items.text: Document the rule or choice for learning curves so another learner can reproduce the analysis and understand its limitations.

items.title: Regularization
items.text: Define regularization in relation to overfitting and underfitting; identify the input, output, assumptions, and who uses the result.

content_blocks.title: Guided walkthrough
content_blocks.text: 1. Restate the question addressed by overfitting and underfitting. 2. Identify the input data, intended output, and assumptions. 3. Predict what the small example should show before reading its output. 4. Change one input or assumption, compare the result, and document what remains uncertain.

content_blocks.code:
actual = [3, 5, 8]
predicted = [4, 4, 7]
mae = sum(abs(a-p) for a,p in zip(actual,predicted))/len(actual)
print("MAE:", round(mae, 2))

For SQL, adapt the query to an approved local schema; the stated result is a conceptual query simulation, not a live database result.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Restore the provided synthetic input, rerun or retrace the example, and change one value at a time. Do not use personal records, credentials, or data you are not authorized to access.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Keep the question, data grain, units, and assumptions explicit. If a result differs, inspect the input and steps in order. Avoid turning an observed association into a causal claim, treating a sample as the population, or assuming a small demonstration guarantees production behavior. Always compare with a simple baseline and choose a metric that fits the use case.

content_blocks.title: Responsible interpretation
content_blocks.text: This example is a teaching aid. It is static in the CodeLeaf lesson and is not executed in the browser. It uses small synthetic values; validate any real workflow in a separate, appropriate local environment and protect sensitive data.

content_blocks.title: Recap and next step
content_blocks.text: Recap: Machine learning estimates patterns from examples. Training is only one step: a robust workflow defines splits, baselines, metrics, assumptions, and monitoring. Next, connect this lesson to the linked prerequisite or following lesson. Record the method, input assumptions, observed result, and one limitation so another person can reproduce and review the work.

content.task: Try it yourself: create a small synthetic example for overfitting and underfitting. State a question, make a prediction, trace or run an appropriate calculation, then write one finding and one limitation.
task_acceptance_criteria: Refer accurately to the topic and its syllabus subtopics.
Record a reproducible example or a complete manual trace with an expected result.
Document at least one assumption, limitation, data-quality issue, or evaluation check.
hints: Write down the input, expected result, units, and assumptions first.
Change only one condition when testing a revised example.
Ask whether the data and method represent the real decision; do not infer causality or production readiness from a toy example.
troubleshooting: Check input values, path assumptions, package versions, indentation, and units.
For SQL, use a local schema and read-only test data; this page does not provide a live database.
For package-dependent work, create an isolated environment and use the relevant official documentation.
